source: 外研社必修一 Unit 2 同主题完形(汉堡疑问/初遇美式词/像搭积木造词/网上聊天/晚餐误会/学习习语)。用词限 U2/初中/常见词,答案唯一,与阅读关不撞文章。答案位由 _balance 打散。

passages.title: A Boy and His Hamburger
passages.text: One afternoon my little brother held up his lunch and asked me a very (1)____ question: was there really ham inside a hamburger? I started to laugh, because of course there (2)____. His question made me notice how (3)____ English can be. There is no egg in an eggplant, and a pineapple has neither pine nor apple in it. The more examples I thought of, the more (4)____ they seemed. We sculpt a sculpture, but we just (5)____ a photo. We say it is (6)____ when water falls from the sky, yet we never say it is 'sunshining'. I told my brother that English was (7)____ by people, not by computers, so it is full of surprises. He listened with wide eyes and then asked another funny (8)____. That evening I realised that his simple questions had (9)____ me to look at my own language in a new way. Sometimes a child can (10)____ you something important.

passages.title: My First Day with American Words
passages.text: On my first day in New York, I quickly learned that American and British English are not the (1)____. When my host asked me to put 'gas' in the car, I was (2)____, because in Britain we call it petrol. Then he said we would drive along the (3)____, which I knew as the motorway at home. Later we took the (4)____ to the top of a tall building; my family in London would have said 'lift'. To get across the city, we rode the (5)____, but in the UK people travel on the underground. That night I went back to my small (6)____, the kind of home an American would call an apartment. So many everyday (7)____ were different that my head was spinning. Luckily, my host could always guess my (8)____ from the situation, so we never had any real (9)____. By the end of the week, I could even (10)____ the two kinds of English apart, and the whole thing felt like a fun game.

passages.title: Building Words Like Blocks
passages.text: My English teacher once told us that making new words is a bit like (1)____ with blocks. Many long words are simply (2)____ from shorter ones we already know. The first way, she said, is to (3)____ two words together, so 'home' and 'work' give us 'homework'. The second way is to add a (4)____ or a suffix. If we put 'un-' in front of 'happy', the new word means the (5)____. If we add '-ment' to 'improve', we get a (6)____ called 'improvement'. The third way is to use a word as a different (7)____ of speech, the way we 'water' the plants. Once I understood these (8)____, reading became much easier. Whenever I met an (9)____ word, I broke it into parts and tried to guess its meaning. My teacher was right: knowing how words are built can really (10)____ you when you read.

passages.title: Chatting with My Online Friend
passages.text: Last year I made a foreign friend on a learning (1)____, and we often chat online in English. At first, his messages were full of short forms that I could not (2)____. When he typed 'BRB', I had no idea he meant 'be right (3)____'. He also used 'COZ' instead of 'because', just to (4)____ time. Slowly, I got used to this kind of (5)____ language and even started to use it myself. But my friend gave me one piece of good (6)____: before sending such words, I should think about who would (7)____ them. With close friends they are clear and friendly, but a teacher might not (8)____ what I mean. So now I am more (9)____ of my reader. Learning to chat online has not only improved my English; it has also (10)____ me that the right words depend on the right situation.

passages.title: A Surprising Dinner
passages.text: Last summer I stayed with a kind British (1)____. One evening, the mother smiled and said we would have 'toad-in-the-hole' for (2)____. I was really (3)____, because I thought a toad was a kind of animal like a frog. Why would anyone (4)____ a toad? I did not want to be (5)____, so I said nothing and waited nervously. To my (6)____, the dish turned out to be sausages baked in a kind of cake, and it was (7)____! Everyone laughed when I explained what I had (8)____ at first. The funny name had completely (9)____ me. After that night, I learned never to judge an English dish by its strange (10)____, and I happily tried everything the family offered.

passages.title: Learning Tricky Expressions
passages.text: My favourite English lesson was the day our teacher taught us some (1)____ expressions that do not mean what they seem. She said that if someone has 'a frog in their (2)____', it does not mean they ate a frog; they just cannot speak (3)____ for a moment. If a friend has 'green fingers', their hands are not really (4)____; they are simply good at growing (5)____. When your mother tells you to 'pull up your (6)____', she is not talking about your clothes; she wants you to try (7)____. The teacher also warned us that in Britain, the (8)____ 'Not bad' is often real praise. It can mean something is rather (9)____, better than expected.
